title: Joel
subtitle: Yoel, “The LORD is God”
description: A short, urgent book that begins with a plague of locusts stripping the land bare and hears in it the coming day of the LORD. Joel calls priests and farmers, elders and children to a holy fast — “Tear your hearts, not your clothes” — and in answer God sends back the rain, promises to make up for the years the locust has eaten, and makes the promise Peter quoted at Pentecost: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all people.” It ends in the valley of decision, with the LORD roaring from Zion and a spring flowing from his house. Set out line by line as the poetry it is, in the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Joel?
qa.answer: The second of the twelve shorter prophetic books of the Old Testament, three chapters long in English Bibles. It begins with a devastating plague of locusts, calls the people to fast and return to the LORD, and turns at 2:18 from lament to promise: rain and harvest restored, the Spirit poured out on all people, the nations judged, and the LORD dwelling in Zion. Its great theme is the day of the LORD, the day when God acts to judge and to save.

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Joel, and when?
qa.answer: The book opens, “The LORD’s word came to Joel son of Pethuel” (1:1), and nothing more is known of him. Unlike most prophets he names no king, so his date is uncertain. Some scholars place him early, in the ninth century BC; many place him after the return from exile in Babylon, perhaps around 400 BC, pointing to the role of elders and priests and the mention of the Greeks (3:6); others date him in between. The book’s message does not depend on the answer.

qa.question: What is the day of the LORD in Joel?
qa.answer: The day when God intervenes in history to judge evil and rescue his people. Joel sees a foretaste of it in the locust plague (“the day of the LORD is close at hand”, 1:15) and warns that it is first a day of darkness for Judah itself, “great and very terrible” (2:11). But for those who return to him it becomes a day of rescue: “all who call on the name of the LORD will be saved” (2:32). In chapter 3 it is the day when the nations are judged in the valley of decision.

qa.question: Is the army in Joel 2 locusts or soldiers?
qa.answer: Readers have answered in different ways. Some think chapter 2 describes the same locust plague as chapter 1, pictured as an invading army; others think it is a human army, perhaps the “northern army” of 2:20, of which the locusts were a warning; others see in it the hosts of the final day of the LORD. Joel himself calls the locusts God’s “great army” (2:25), and the poem may hold all three together, the present disaster opening a window onto the last one.

qa.question: How is Joel connected with Pentecost?
qa.answer: On the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came on the first disciples and they spoke in other languages, Peter told the crowd, “this is what was spoken through the prophet Joel” (Acts 2:16), and quoted Joel 2:28–32: “I will pour out my Spirit upon all people. Your sons and your daughters will prophesy”. Paul quotes its last line, that all who call on the name of the Lord will be saved, in Romans 10:13. Christians read the promise as fulfilled in the gift of the Spirit to the whole church.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Hebrew beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
